stories.headline: STOCKS BOUNCE 0.35% AS MONEY ROTATES OUT OF AI INTO BANKS AND HEALTHCARE
stories.body: The S&P 500 recovered 0.35% to 7,746 and the Dow jumped 1.08% to 52,177.69, a day after a hot September CPI (headline +3.7% y/y, core +2.6%) triggered the Nasdaq's worst session since July. Today's gain was narrow and defensive: the Dow outpaced the Nasdaq roughly 5-to-1 as traders sold richly valued AI infrastructure names and bought banks coming off strong earnings and beaten-down healthcare stocks.
stories.explain: A rotation day like this is a signal about positioning, not the economy — when a hot CPI print raises the odds the Fed holds rates higher for longer, the stocks that get hit hardest are the ones priced for years of future growth, since a higher discount rate shrinks the present value of those distant earnings the most. Money has to go somewhere, so it flows into sectors like banks (which benefit directly from higher rates via wider net interest margins) and defensive healthcare names whose cash flows are already near-term, which is exactly the Dow-over-Nasdaq pattern that showed up today.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD RETREATS TO 5.09% AS TECH SELLOFF DRIVES A FLIGHT TO BONDS
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield fell roughly 10 bps to about 5.09%, unwinding most of Wednesday's spike to 5.33% after the hot CPI report, as the AI-stock selloff pushed investors back into safe-haven Treasurys. The 30-year yield dropped more than 9 bps to 5.43%, while traders still price at least one more quarter-point Fed hike by year-end following September's first hike in three years.
stories.explain: Yields and equities are fighting two different forces right now: CPI-driven inflation fear pushes yields up by raising the expected Fed path, while an equity-risk-off day pulls yields back down as investors sell stocks and buy bonds for safety, mechanically bidding up bond prices and pushing yields lower. Today the risk-off force won out over the inflation force, which is why yields fell on the same day the CPI reaction was still working through the system — a reminder that a single day's yield move can reflect a very different mechanism than the day before's.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS GAINS AS HOUTHI MISSILE STRIKES ARAMCO INFRASTRUCTURE IN DHAHRAN
stories.body: Brent crude climbed to roughly $106.33/bbl and WTI to about $94.73 after a Houthi missile struck an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, and UKMTO reported two more tanker strikes in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran's parliament speaker says traffic stays restricted until Washington meets a list of conditions. Analysts describe the move as a pure risk-premium repricing — no confirmed physical supply has been lost yet.
stories.explain: Oil's risk premium is the gap between today's price and what fundamentals (actual supply and demand) alone would justify, and it exists because markets price in the probability-weighted cost of a worse outcome — a full Hormuz closure that would remove roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil supply. That premium is why a single missile strike with no measurable barrel lost can still move Brent several dollars: traders aren't pricing today's damage, they're pricing the rising odds of tomorrow's.

stories.headline: BANK OF AMERICA AND MORGAN STANLEY ROUND OUT A MIXED BIG-BANK EARNINGS WEEK
stories.body: Bank of America and Morgan Stanley reported Wednesday into the CPI shock, following Citigroup's $2.85 and Wells Fargo's $1.87 EPS beats and JPMorgan's $5.57 miss against a $5.93 consensus earlier in the week. Bank stocks were among today's biggest gainers as the sector benefits from both the earnings beats and the rotation out of AI names.
stories.explain: Banks are one of the few sectors that can win on both sides of this week's story: a hotter CPI print that keeps the Fed's policy rate elevated widens the spread between what banks charge on loans and pay on deposits, directly lifting net interest income, while today's rotation out of expensive growth stocks is giving financials a relative-value bid on top of that. The open question the market hasn't resolved is whether a rate-driven slowdown eventually hurts loan demand and credit quality enough to offset the margin benefit.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TOPS PRESEASON TOP 25 AS MICHIGAN AND UCONN OPEN NEW ERAS WITH TIP-OFF THREE WEEKS AWAY
stories.body: With the Nov. 2 opener roughly three weeks out, ESPN's preseason Top 25 projects Florida at No. 1, while KenPom's model favors Duke. Reigning champion Michigan and runner-up UConn both enter the season under heavy roster turnover, and the AP's official preseason poll has not yet been released.

stories.headline: LAKERS' RECORD $12 BILLION SALE CLOSES AS LUKA DONCIC SITS OUT INDEFINITELY
stories.body: ESPN reports the Lakers' ownership sale has closed at a record $12 billion NBA valuation, even as the team opens the preseason without Luka Doncic — ruled out indefinitely by coach JJ Redick — and with LeBron James reportedly managing chronic arthritis. Elsewhere, 18-year veteran Russell Westbrook announced his retirement, and the NBA Cup group-stage schedule kicks off Oct. 30 with the Lakers at the Warriors.

stories.headline: 49ERS STAY UNBEATEN AT 5-0; SEAHAWKS HOST THURSDAY NIGHT SHOWDOWN AT BRONCOS TONIGHT
stories.body: San Francisco improved to 5-0 Sunday, rallying from a fourth-quarter deficit to beat Seattle 32-29 and drop the Seahawks to 3-2. Seattle visits Denver tonight for Thursday Night Football (8:15 p.m. ET), with both teams debuting throwback uniforms for the Week 6 matchup.

stories.headline: GEORGIA HOLDS NO. 1 IN AP POLL AS HUSKIES DROP TO 3-3 AHEAD OF FRIDAY AT PURDUE
stories.body: Georgia (6-0) remains No. 1 in this week's AP Top 25 with Notre Dame, Miami, Ohio State, and Indiana rounding out the top five, while Texas and Oregon continue to slide. Washington fell to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten) in a blowout loss to No. 20 Iowa and visits Purdue Friday, Oct. 16 — the Huskies' first trip to West Lafayette since 1990.

sports.detail: Dealt reserve center Isaiah Stewart to Memphis for three future second-round picks and used the No. 17 pick on Stanford guard Ebuka Okorie, who's seeing early backcourt minutes. Split their first two preseason games (beat Phoenix, lost in OT at Washington); at Minnesota tonight, host Toronto Oct. 16, then open the regular season Oct. 20 vs. Boston defending last year's 60-22, East's No. 1 seed finish.

Fell to 3-2 after blowing a 26-21 fourth-quarter lead to the unbeaten 49ers (5-0) on Sunday. Next: tonight, Oct. 15 at Denver Broncos, 8:15 p.m. ET (TNF), both teams in throwback uniforms.
Dropped to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten) in a blowout home loss to No. 20 Iowa; starter Demond Williams Jr. left with an injury. Next: Friday, Oct. 16 at Purdue — UW's first trip there since 1990.

Exhibition at Boise State is Oct. 17, home vs. Washington State Oct. 25, then the opener vs. Colgate Nov. 2 and a return to the Maui Invitational Nov. 23 vs. BYU.

deepDive.title: Why Yields Fell and the Dow Beat the Nasdaq on the Same CPI-Driven Day
content: Today's brief contains what looks like a contradiction: a hot CPI print that should push yields higher is sitting next to a 10-year yield that fell about 10 bps, while the Dow rallied more than 1% and the AI-heavy Nasdaq barely moved. Both are true at once, and reconciling them says something important about how markets process a single data point over several days rather than one. Wednesday's price action was pure inflation repricing — yields spiked to 5.33% and growth stocks sold off because a higher expected Fed path raises the discount rate applied to future profits. Today's price action was a second-order reaction to that first move, and the two can point in opposite directions even though they share the same root cause.

The mechanism is a rotation out of crowded, highly valued positions and into safety and value. When AI infrastructure stocks had already absorbed the worst of the discount-rate hit on Wednesday, some of Thursday's selling in that same group reflected investors de-risking further rather than reacting to new information — and the money leaving those positions needed somewhere to go. Some flowed into Treasurys, which is a flight-to-safety bid that pushes bond prices up and yields down regardless of the inflation outlook; some flowed into banks and healthcare, sectors whose earnings are nearer-term and less sensitive to the discount-rate math driving AI valuations. That's the exact mechanism behind the Dow's roughly 5-to-1 outperformance over the Nasdaq today.

What's easy to miss is that this isn't really a story about the Fed changing its mind — futures markets still imply the same elevated odds of a year-end hike that they did Wednesday night. It's a story about how concentrated the AI trade has become: when a single catalyst like CPI makes expensive growth stocks wobble, the subsequent unwind can be large relative to the news itself, because so much capital was positioned the same way. The 2000 dot-com unwind is the extreme historical version of this dynamic — a sector trading on years-out earnings expectations where even a modest rate or growth scare triggered outsized, self-reinforcing selling once the first cracks appeared.

For Chris's kind of analysis, the useful takeaway is to separate the signal from the noise across consecutive sessions: Wednesday's yield spike told you about inflation expectations, while today's yield retreat told you about equity positioning, not inflation expectations reversing. Watching whether the 10-year stabilizes near 5.1% or resumes climbing toward Wednesday's 5.33% high over the next few sessions will reveal which force — the CPI-driven rate path or the AI-stock de-risking — is actually in control heading into the Oct. 28-29 FOMC meeting.
